review_notes:
I read the whole target file (245 lines) and all of its declarations, then checked the relevant Mathlib sources: Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/DSlope.lean, Mathlib/Analysis/Analytic/IsolatedZeros.lean, Mathlib/Analysis/Analytic/Order.lean, Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/IteratedDeriv/Defs.lean, Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/Taylor.lean, and Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/FDeriv/Analytic.lean. I also checked downstream uses in LeanPool/JacobianDiffgeo/ResidueCalculus/{LaurentCoeff,PrincipalPart,Residue}.lean and MeromorphicTrace/PlanarTrace.lean.

The file contains exactly one new definition, `RS.taylorCoeffAt` (lines 42-43). It has no structure, instance or typeclass declaration. The closest Mathlib notions are (i) `taylorCoeffWithin` (Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/Taylor.lean:62), which is genuinely restricted to `ℝ → E` and within-set derivatives, (ii) the coefficient of the canonical power series `FormalMultilinearSeries.ofScalars 𝕜 (fun n => iteratedDeriv n f x / n.factorial)` produced by `AnalyticAt.hasFPowerSeriesAt` (Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/IteratedDeriv/Defs.lean:339-342), and (iii) `FormalMultilinearSeries.coeff`. On analytic `g` these all encode the same number, and the target proves the bridge to the power-series coefficient (`HasFPowerSeriesAt.taylorCoeffAt_eq`, lines 56-62). However, `taylorCoeffAt` is a documented, deliberately different representation (`no iteratedDeriv, no factorials`, lines 20-22 and 39-41), it has a substantial used API across the residue-calculus files, and the rubric explicitly says that a named API built on a chosen different representation or generic operation is not redundant merely because it can be expressed using existing operations. I therefore did not treat the definition as an avoidable competing concept.

The other near-match is `AnalyticAt.exists_taylor_remainder` (lines 195-243) against Mathlib's `AnalyticAt.exists_eq_sum_add_pow_mul` (Mathlib/Analysis/Analytic/Order.lean:416-419). The latter is the same exact pointwise Taylor factorization, but centered at 0 and phrased with `iteratedDeriv i f 0 / i.factorial`; the target is centered at an arbitrary `z₀` and additionally asserts the shifted-coefficient property `∀ j, taylorCoeffAt r z₀ j = taylorCoeffAt g z₀ (j + m)`, which is actually consumed downstream (e.g. `hrcoeff` in PrincipalPart.lean:127-131). This is theorem duplication / a genuine generalization, which the rubric excludes ('Exclude standalone theorem duplication and proof shortening'), so I abstained.

The remaining declarations are either thin named specialisations (`AnalyticAt.iterate_dslope`, a one-step packaging of `HasFPowerSeriesAt.has_fpower_series_iterate_dslope_fslope`), missing lemmas for Mathlib's `dslope` API (`Filter.EventuallyEq.dslope_eq`, `dslope_const_mul`, `dslope_const`, `dslope_sub_mul`; no corresponding declarations exist in Mathlib's DSlope.lean), or the linearity/monomial API for the new definition. These are theorem-level API, not competing definitions.

Remaining uncertainty: if the project wants maximal reuse of Mathlib's `iteratedDeriv` and analytic-order machinery, a useful (not rubric-mandated) addition would be a bridge lemma `taylorCoeffAt g z₀ j = iteratedDeriv j g z₀ / (j! : ℂ)` for analytic `g`, or a note that the general-`z₀` remainder theorem subsumes Mathlib's order-theoretic Taylor theorem after change of origin. Neither rises to an avoidable duplicated concept under this rubric, because the existing definition is an intentional, documented representation and the remainder theorem has genuinely extra content.
